---
title: "How conspiratorial claims acquire political authority"
subtitle: "A dissertation in progress · Political Science, Georgia State University"
---

## The question

Which conspiratorial allegations circulating on fringe platforms are taken up by U.S. political elites, what do intermediaries (podcasts, alt-video, cable) do to those allegations on the way, and does a claim's attributed origin change whether the public accepts a politician using it?

## The argument, in one paragraph

Allegations leave the fringe carrying a stigma. Somewhere between an imageboard and a debate stage the stigma comes off: the wording is recoded, the messenger changes, and the source is replaced by "people are saying." I call this laundering and treat it as a mechanism to test, not a label. The dissertation builds a cohort of claims that includes the ones that went nowhere, asks which claims elites selected and whether laundered versions were selected more, and tests experimentally whether hiding a claim's origin raises political acceptability more than it raises belief.
